title: Governing law: Classification precedes contract analysis
desc: Separates doctrinal recall, issue recognition and resource-based application, treating automated classification as a narrow proposed legal-AI use.

kps.k: Governing-law recognition links professional examination requirements with a narrow test of AI legal reasoning.
kps.d: The NextGen UBE scope for July 2026–February 2027 requires examinees to distinguish common-law, UCC Article 2 and hybrid transactions. LegalBench isolates part of that competence in a manually constructed task containing 100 simple contract descriptions, asking models to classify each under the UCC or common law. The shared focus concerns identifying the applicable legal framework, not demonstrating comprehensive contract-law competence.

qs.a: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models · Academia · 2023

kps.k: The examination distinguishes doctrinal recall, issue recognition and resource-based application rather than treating them as interchangeable skills.
kps.d: NextGen UBE tests starred topics without legal resources. For unstarred topics, examinees must recognise relevant issues from memory when resources are absent and efficiently analyse and apply resources when supplied. Contracts questions use Foundational Skills tasks and may cross subject areas. The practical preparation implication is to develop both retained knowledge and resource-use skills; the outline does not establish that either can replace the other.

kps.k: Classification matters because the governing framework changes substantive contract analysis.
kps.d: LegalBench motivates the task through differences in gap-filling, option consideration, merchant firm offers and modification rules. NextGen UBE places governing-law identification within broader coverage of formation, enforceability, interpretation, performance, breach and remedies. Together, these materials explain why classification is a consequential preliminary step, while distinguishing it from applying the resulting rules to a dispute.

kps.k: The central qualification is a difference in scope, not an expressed disagreement about AI capability.
kps.d: LegalBench excludes mixed goods-and-services contracts, whereas NextGen UBE includes hybrid transactions and may supply resources for them. LegalBench acknowledges that real-world mixed-purpose classification can be difficult and costly to litigate. Its authors predict near-perfect lawyer performance on the simple task but do not report a measured human baseline or model scores in the supplied material. NextGen UBE specifies examination requirements rather than empirical findings and warns that detailed scope descriptions do not indicate testing priority. Neither excerpt establishes equivalence between benchmark success and professional competence.

qs.q: Each description is followed the question, “Is this contract governed by the UCC or the common law?” The dataset does not include “mixed purpose” contracts which incorporate both the sale of a good and a service.

kps.k: Automated contract sorting and harder classification benchmarks remain proposed applications.
kps.d: LegalBench suggests subject-matter sorting for contract lifecycle management review and presents the simple task as a starting point for mixed-purpose classification. These are prospective uses, not demonstrated deployment outcomes. The practical distinction is between organising contracts for review and resolving the more demanding governing-law questions that the current task leaves out.

qs.q: Third, this task could prove useful in the context of contract lifecycle management (CLM) in which a CLM software product could automatically sort contracts by subject matter for review purposes.

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research source supports the proposition that governing-law classification is a consequential preliminary step but only a narrow test of legal-AI reasoning. LegalBench isolates simple UCC-versus-common-law classification, while excluding mixed-purpose contracts that better reflect the harder boundary questions encountered in practice. Its doctrinal discussion supports the proposition that classification matters because the applicable framework changes the substantive rules. At the same time, the source does not establish broader professional competence: it reports neither model scores nor a measured human baseline, and presents automated contract sorting and mixed-purpose classification as prospective applications. Internal variation is therefore one of scope rather than direction—the source advances possible uses beyond the elementary benchmark while expressly recognising that real-world classification is harder. This assessment concerns this supplied source, not academia or legal-AI research generally.

vlens.an: The regulator and professional-body evidence supports the proposition’s legal-practice core: governing-law classification is treated as a preliminary contracts competence, specifically distinguishing common law, UCC Article 2 and hybrid transactions. It also supports the proposition’s separation of recalled doctrine, issue recognition and resource-based application by expressly requiring efficient analysis and application when resources are supplied. The material does not, however, evaluate LegalBench, model performance or automated contract sorting, so it supports the doctrinal and competency framing without substantiating the proposition’s AI-related applications. Because the curated evidence contains only the NextGen UBE scope document, it reveals no material internal variation within this professional voice and should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 LegalBench source supports the proposition that governing-law classification is a consequential preliminary step but only a narrow test of legal-AI reasoning, not evidence of comprehensive contract-analysis competence. It connects classification to substantive differences between UCC and common-law rules, while limiting the benchmark to simple contracts and excluding mixed-purpose transactions. Its broader claims introduce some internal variation: subject-matter sorting, contract-lifecycle-management use, and a harder mixed-purpose benchmark are presented as possible extensions, while near-perfect lawyer performance is predicted rather than measured. The supplied material also reports no model scores. These qualifications reinforce, rather than undermine, the cluster’s distinction between classification, doctrinal application, and demonstrated professional competence.

elens.an: The sole curated 2025 source supports the proposition’s legal and competency framing: governing-law classification is treated as a preliminary requirement that distinguishes common law, UCC Article 2 and hybrid transactions, while resource-based analysis and application are assessed separately. This reinforces the proposition that classification is narrower than full contract analysis and that recalled doctrine, issue recognition and resource use are distinct skills. Materially, however, the source is an examination specification rather than evidence of legal-AI performance, deployment or adoption at scale. It therefore does not validate LegalBench results, automated classification capability or real-world uptake; nor does it establish equivalence between successful sorting and professional competence. Because only one curated source is supplied for this period, its position should not be treated as representative of a wider group.
